Sound Waves

Let us consider a situation where one person is speaking into a microphone while the other person is receiving sound through speakers as illustrated in the figure 3.1.
modelAnswer: A person speaking into a microphone produces sound waves, which are analog signals.
The microphone captures these sound waves.
An ADC converts the analog signal into digital data.
The digital data can be transmitted over long distances with little or no degradation in quality.
At the receiver, a DAC converts the digital signals back into analog signals.
The speakers translate these analog signals into sound waves.
The listener hears the other person's voice.

explain.title: Analog signals
explain.body: Analog signals are signals that changes with time smoothly and continuously over time. They can have any value within given range. Examples include voice signal (speaking), body's temperature and radio-wave signals.

explain.title: Digital signals
explain.body: Digital signals are the signals which have only two values that are in the form of '0' and '1'. These are utilized in digital electronics and computing systems.

explain.title: ADC and DAC
explain.body: Analog to Digital Conversion (ADC): ADC is the conversion of analog signals into digital signals, which are discrete and can be easily processed by computerized devices like computers and smart phones. Digital to Analog Conversion (DAC): DAC is the conversion whereby analog signals are converted to digital signals, making it possible for human to perceive the information, for instance through speakers, as depicted in figure 3. 1.

explain.title: Digital logic and logic levels
explain.body: Digital logic uses binary numbers, 0 and 1, to represent and manipulate information. In digital circuits, the two states are represented by different voltage levels. Conventionally, a higher voltage such as 5 volts refers to binary 1, while a low voltage such as 0 volts refers to binary 0. These voltage levels are called logic levels.

mistakes: Do not reverse ADC and DAC: ADC means analog to digital, while DAC means digital to analog.
Do not describe analog signals as having only 0 and 1; that is the description of digital signals.
Do not say digital signals have infinitely many possible values; the section describes them as having two values.
When writing the microphone-to-speaker process, do not leave out either converter.
Do not reverse the conventional logic levels: 5 volts represents 1, and 0 volts represents 0.

explain.title: Binary variables
explain.body: Binary variables have only two possible values: 0 and 1. In logic, these may also be described as False and True.

explain.title: AND, OR and NOT
explain.body: AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT takes one input and gives its opposite.

explain.title: Boolean functions
explain.body: A Boolean function is a function which has a one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output. It is built using logic operations such as AND, OR and NOT.

explain.title: Truth tables and logic gates
explain.body: A truth table shows the output for every possible input combination. Logic gates are physical devices in electronic circuits that perform Boolean operations.

mistakes: Do not confuse AND and OR: AND needs both inputs to be 1, while OR needs at least one input to be 1.
Do not leave out an input combination when making a truth table.
For NOT, reverse the input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0.
When evaluating a multi-part function, calculate each operation column before the final output column.
In Boolean logic, 1 + 1 for OR is 1, not 2.

writtenQuestions.text: Simplify the expression A + A̅ · B.
modelAnswer: A + A̅ · B = (A + A̅) · (A + B) (Distributive Law)
= 1 · (A + B) (Complement Law)
= A + B (Identity Law)

writtenQuestions.text: Simplify the expression A̅·B̅ + A̅ · B.

rubric.how: Simplify A̅ · 1 to A̅.

modelAnswer: (A + B) · (A + B̅) = A·(A+B̅)+B·(A+B̅) (Distributive Law)
= A + A·B̅ + B·B̅ (Distributive Law and Absorption Law)

explain.title: What simplification means
explain.body: Simplification means applying of some Boolean algebra rules to make the functions less complicated. A shorter function can need fewer gates in its digital circuit.

explain.title: Useful basic laws
explain.body: Remember the identities A + 0 = A and A · 1 = A; the complements A + A̅ = 1 and A · A̅ = 0; and the absorption laws A + (A · B) = A and A · (A + B) = A.

explain.title: De Morgan's theorems
explain.body: When a whole bracket is complemented, change OR to AND and complement each variable: (A + B)̅ = A̅ · B̅. For a complemented product, change AND to OR: (A · B)̅ = A̅ + B̅.

explain.title: Show your working
explain.body: Use one valid rule at a time and write the new expression on the next line. This makes your method easy to follow and helps you earn working marks.

mistakes: Do not confuse + (OR) with · (AND); they have different laws.
When applying De Morgan's theorem, complement every variable and change the operation inside the bracket.
Do not skip steps when factoring or expanding; a missing or incorrect term can lose working marks.
Do not stop at an expression that can still be reduced by a complement or absorption law.
Write the final simplified expression clearly and keep its variables and complements correct.

explain.title: Binary signals and Boolean functions
explain.body: Digital systems use binary values, 0 and 1. A Boolean function describes how input values determine an output, for example F(A, B) = A + B.

explain.title: Logic gates and truth tables
explain.body: AND, OR, and NOT gates carry out Boolean operations. A truth table lists every possible input combination and the output for each one.

explain.title: Boolean laws and duality
explain.body: Boolean laws help simplify expressions. To form a dual, interchange + and ·, and interchange 0 and 1; for example, the dual of A · 0 = 0 is A + 1 = 1.

explain.title: Adders
explain.body: A half-adder adds two bits: Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B. A full-adder also adds an input carry: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = A · B + A · Cin + B · Cin.

explain.title: Karnaugh maps
explain.body: A Karnaugh map arranges output values so adjacent 1s can be grouped. Each larger valid group can remove variables and produce a simpler expression.

mistakes: Do not confuse Boolean OR (+) with arithmetic addition; it outputs 1 if at least one input is 1.
Do not use XOR as a synonym for OR: XOR outputs 1 only when its inputs differ.
When forming a dual, interchange both operators (+ and ·) and constants (0 and 1).
Do not omit input combinations from a truth table.
In a half-adder, the carry is A · B and the sum is A ⊕ B; do not swap them.
When simplifying, keep complements attached to the correct variables and show each law-based step.

notes.title: Analog and Digital Signals
notes.answer: An ADC converts analog signals into digital signals.
notes.explanation: An analog signal changes smoothly and can take any value in a range. A digital signal has only two possible values, 0 and 1. An ADC changes an analog signal into digital form; a DAC changes digital data back into an analog signal.
notes.simple: Analog is smooth and can have many values. Digital uses just 0 and 1. ADC changes analog to digital; DAC changes digital to analog.
examples: A voice entering a microphone is an analog signal; an ADC converts it into digital data.
A DAC converts digital data into an analog signal that a speaker turns into sound.
steps: A microphone captures sound waves, which are analog signals.
An ADC converts the analog signal into digital data made of 0s and 1s.
The digital data can be processed, stored, or transmitted.
A DAC changes the digital data back into an analog signal.
A speaker turns the analog signal into sound waves.
notes.checkQuestion: Which converter changes an analog signal into a digital signal?
notes.checkAnswer: An ADC converts analog signals into digital signals.

notes.title: Boolean functions and basic logic
notes.answer: A Boolean function uses binary inputs and logic operations to produce a binary output.
notes.explanation: A Boolean function takes one or more binary inputs and gives one binary output. Its inputs and output are only 0 or 1. AND, OR and NOT are used to build Boolean functions.
notes.simple: A Boolean function is a rule that takes in 0s and 1s and gives back a 0 or 1.
examples: For F(A, B) = A · B, the output is 1 only when A = 1 and B = 1.
For P = ¬A, if A = 1 then P = 0.
steps: Write the input values: A = 0 and B = 1.
For AND, the output is 1 only if both inputs are 1, so A · B = 0.
For OR, the output is 1 if at least one input is 1, so A + B = 1.
notes.checkQuestion: If A = 0 and B = 1, what are A · B and A + B?
notes.checkAnswer: For A = 1 and B = 0, A · B = 0 and A + B = 1.

notes.title: Simplifying Boolean Functions
notes.explanation: Boolean simplification uses algebra rules to make a function shorter while keeping the same output. For example, A + A·B = A by the absorption law. Another example is A + A̅·B = A + B, using the distributive, complement and identity laws.
notes.simple: Use Boolean rules to remove unnecessary parts of an expression without changing its value.
steps: Look for a pair or pattern that matches a Boolean law.
Apply one law at a time and show its name if required.
Continue until no part can be simplified further.

notes.answer: A half-adder produces its carry using the AND operation: Carry = A · B.
notes.explanation: Boolean algebra works with two values, 0 and 1. It describes how logic gates combine binary inputs to produce binary outputs.
notes.simple: Think of Boolean algebra as rules for working with switches that are either off (0) or on (1).
examples: If F = A + B, then F is 1 whenever at least one input is 1.
For a half-adder, Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B.

quiz.stem: Using the identity law, what is A + 0?

0 is wrong because the identity law does not replace A with 0.

quiz.stem: What is the value of A + A̅?
rationales: A is wrong because the complement law gives 1 for A + A̅.
0 is wrong because A · A̅, not A + A̅, equals 0.

quiz.stem: Simplify A · (A + B).
rationales: A is correct by the absorption law A · (A + B) = A.
B is wrong because the expression does not reduce to B.
A + B is wrong because the absorption law removes the extra B term.

quiz.stem: By De Morgan's theorem, what is (A + B)̅?

A̅ · B̅ is correct by De Morgan's theorem.
A + B is wrong because it has no complements.

quiz.stem: Simplify A + A̅ · B.

A is wrong because the expression can be 1 when A = 0 and B = 1.

quiz.stem: Simplify A̅ · B̅ + A̅ · B.
rationales: A̅ is correct because factoring A̅ gives A̅ · (B̅ + B) = A̅.
B is wrong because the expression is 1 whenever A = 0, regardless of B.
A̅ + B̅ is wrong because the expression is 0 when A = 1 and B = 0.
